The ports of Vera Cruz and Tampico will remain entirely free for the entrance and departure of neutral non commercial mail packets. Mexican boats engaged exclusively in fishing, on any part of the coast, will be allowed to pursue their labors unmolested. Uses of Salt. þÿ A correspondent in the Morning Chronicle quotes a letter received from a gentleman ill the United States, who is an extensive farmer there, in which it is shown that salt applied to land previous to being ploughed for potato setting has the very best eti'ect. Having suffered a loss of (tie greater portion of a crop in 1844 he, in the spring of 1845, determined to attempt the growth of another crop from the same held. He accordingly, before ploughing, had a hundred and a half weight of medium coarse salt per acre spread broadcast, and then left one or two weeks, that it might dissolve and mix with the soil. The usual method of culture was then pursued, and a fair crop of excellent quality was obtained, not a diseased potato being found when they were got up at harvest time nor had there been one discovered lip to the 28th cd Match, 184G. This, adds the writer, makes three well authenticated cases of the remedial agenev of salt, and even where the plant was repeated in the soil where the previous crop had been diseased. The Agricultural Ga- I zelle. says þÿ In Cheshire there is a farm on which there is a salt spring, to which the cows daily resoit; and this farm is par denial |y noted for the excellence of its cheese, Mini it is believed that the tasting of this brine by the cows adds to the flavour of their þÿmilk.

To listen well is to make an unconscious ad vnncemonl in the power of cotueisiiig. In listening we perceive in what the interst in what the failure ol others consist. We become too, aware of our own delieiences, without having them taught through the me diutn of humiliation. We find ourselves often more ignorant than we could have sup posed it possible. We learh by a very mo derate attention to the sort of topics which please to form a style of our own The art of þÿconversation is an unpleasant phrase The power of conversing well is least agreeable when it assumes the character of an art. In listening, a well-bred gentlewoman will gentle sympathise with the speaker ; or, if needs most be, ditier as gently. Much character is shown in the art of listening Some people appear to be in a violent hiiirv whilst another speaks : they hasten on the person who addresses them, as one would urge on a horse, with "Yes, yes, Very good Ah! Others sit on the full stare, eyes fixed as

those of an owl, upon the speaker. T'mm others, a loud and long laugh is, at intervals produced, and all the company tin tia round to see what was the cause of the merriment But nil these vices of manner may he avoided by a gentle attention and a certain calm dignity of manner based upon a reflective mind and humble spirit.

From the Neu) York Herald, June 27, 1840. TUH PROGRESS OF THE WAR IN MEXICO .

The latest intelligence from the seat of tfvar in Mexico, which was published in yesterday's Herald, is of a very interesting tiat'ire. It appears that the town of Regnosa has surrendered to the American arms without a shot being fired, and that the town of Carfrargo stipulated to surrender in advance of the march of our troops. These proceedings are highly gratifying to the American people It seems that the people of Northern Mexico are willing and happy to come under the protection of our flag. It appears that the Mexican people have confidence in the American General and army, and are willing to put their persons and their property under their care. While matters are going on in this way in the vicinity of AJatamoras, it appears that Arista is concentrating his forces and making a s'nnd at Coma, on the road to Monterey, and within about one hundred miles of the American camp, with a determination to oppose the progress of Gen. Taylor to that place. It does not appear that General Taylor had yet moved from Matamoras, in consequence of the want of suitable transportation to carry on offensive operations ; but as soon as transports should arrive, it was his intention to establish a depot at Camaigo, and take up his line of march to Monterey, unless Ins orders were countermanded The neees saiy transports have undoubtedly arrived, and the probability is, that unless Arista has /vacated his position at Coma. a general engagement hot ween the two armies has taken place. If this has not already taken pi ice,

it will in a short time. Arista w ill concentrate his force, await the arrival of I'aredes, and then, with their united strength, risk another battle at Coma, or Monterey, on t he result of which will depend the further prosecution of the war, or a proposal for peace. We have no doubt that if a battle has occurred, the honor of our arms has not been at all tarnished on the occasion. If Gen. Tavlor Was able to achieve so brilliant a victory as he has with u small handful of men, he certainly can achieve a more biillianl one with the additional troops he has since received, animated as they must be by the eclat gathered from the fields of Palo Mto and lies ica de la Palme. According to his order to the gallant Capt May to charge the Mexican batteries he will take Monterey nolens nolens. We may look for the most exciting news very soon.

On Friday the 2l)lh May the Lord Bishop of Antigua arrived at Tortola on iiis visitation to that portion of his diocCse with which the Danish Islands of St. Croix, and St. Thomas have been always associated. At St George's Church, Tortola, a Confirttialion was held of 12 persons; 10 females and 2 males, and at Virgin Gorda. another of 8 persons; 6 females and 2 males. At St John's, Chiistianstcd, St. Croix, 334 persons were .confirmed ; 233 females and 1(31 males. The Bishop also performed the ceremony of laying the first stone of a building for a Sunday School, which is likely to be soon erected under the care of the iMinistef the llev. F. W. Haw ley. The congregations Were large and attentive, and 555 Communicants received the Lord's Supper on Trinity Sunday. Mr. Hawley has been but lately appointed, and seetn likely to be very successful. At St. Paul's, Prederiksted, at the West end of St. Croix, his Lordship confirmed 255 persons, 184 females and 71 males, and also presided at the Public Examination of the Sunday School, when about 500 Children appeared and acquitted themselves tn a very satisfactory manner. His Loidship was much pleased with the slate of tilings generally in St. Croix, and put ticularly with the improvetnents made daring the last 2 yeats at hrrdeviltsted under the Kev. F. S. Mines, the Congregation having been moslliberal, numheiing stmong the proofs of their munificence, an Asylum for their poorer members, a Parson-

age House (or the Minister, and an expensive Organ now momently expected to arrive, besides large internal additions to the accommodation, comfort and elegance of the Church. The Services were attended by large and attentive Congregations, His Lordship reached St. Thomas on 12th June, and having preached and administered the Lord's Supper on Monday the 14th, held the day following, a confirmation of 88 persons, 72 females and 16 males. The congregation attached to the Church of England in St. Thomas is said to number 1500, and it is Very greatly to be desired that a resident Clergyman should be afforded them In the course of this part of His Lordship's Visitation, marked and kind attention was received trom the Danish Authorities, General Sobotker, Governor General of St. Croix, Governor von Oxholm of St. Thomas, and other persons ol distinction, and much consideration was shown in particular by the Danish Lutheran Minister, the llev, 1. t'. Toldoi lund in St. Thomas in giving up his Church to the English Congregation during His Lordship's stay.

SA XTE FE EXPEDITION- Fort Leavenworth, June 23, U40. f presume that there are now near one thousand volunteers here, a few companies being still daily expected. It is very uncertain at what precise day we may start, some thinking within a few days, and some believing that we cannul leave before ten or twelve days. From conversation, however, which ! have had with some of the officers of ihe staff', it is expected that .Major Claik, who is looked for every moment, will bring with him boih additional cannon and sabres, in which case it is more than probable that we shall leave within two, or at most, three days. As to our probable route, nothing is known. As to what the opposition will be that we may meet in t lie course of our campaign, and especially at Same Fe, the vaguest rumors exist, and most unwarranted speculations are indulged in. Some think it certain that we shall be ordered to the Pacific, and others that we shall be ordered to Chihuahua. There is only one thing to be deduced from all this, that positive information regarding our destination will not he given us, until we are beyond the leach of all influences apt to embarrs-s otir progress or prove deleteiious to discipline and subordination. Fort Bent seems to be the rendezvous of our entire forces, and immense trains of pro. vision waggons are to be sent out, and form a complete line between this place and the encampments of the army. No news has as \ el arrived here respect-
ing the success of Capt. Mooie and his dragoons. ordered to cut oil or stop the Mexican supplies.

From the St. Louis Republican, July 3. Very Late from Sante Fe. þÿ We had the pleasure, yesterday, of greeting Messrs. Charles Bent, St Vrain and Folger, traders to New Mexico þÿ about whom, and their fiiends. much solicitude has been felt, in consequence of the hostile relations existing between the United Slates and Mexico, They reached this port in the Radnor, and from a conversation w ith them, we have arrived at the following facts, of very considciatilc interest to the public at the present time. Mr. Bent left Saute Fe on the 27th of May, Taos on the 3d of June and Fort LScnt on the 12th. When Air. Bent was at Sante Fe nothing was known of the warlike movements on the part of Mexico and the United States, nothing of the battles on the Kio Grande þÿ and of course, no hostile demonstrations were making in New Mexico against our traders or citizens. In a conversation with Arrnijo, the commandant of New Mexico, ho did learn thai Gen Urroa w-as on his route to Saute Fe with a force of front three to five thousand men, gathered in Scnora, Zacalccas and I )urango. The object of this expedition was not stated, if known by Gov. Armijo; but there can he little doubt that the presence of Gov, Uma there at such a time, was lite result

of orders from the Mexican government, and with an intention to resist any invasion from this quartet. There were only 180 troops in Saute Ffc at the lime ai Mr. Bent's departure. Mr. Bent did not see the advance party of the traders, composed of one of the Arrmjos, Spvers. Uolburn and others ; but he learned from a company of about 100 Mexicans, who were out hunting buffalo, that they were met bv ' them at Sand near the Simarone, and 00 « miles from the Arkansas. Thpy were pushing n with great rapidity, travelling at the rate of thirty to forty mih s per day. An express from Independence had informed him of the intention to send a detachment of dragoons to stop the progress of Spvers. as was then understood, hut as we know, of all the traders; and hence the rapiditv of their travelling. So intent were they upon getting along, that a hundred extra mules were purchased, ami when a wagon broke down, it was abandoned in the road, alter transferring the goods to another. Capt- Moore's command of dragoons were met on the 17th, between 'he 1 awnee Fork, and the ('aches of the Aikansas. He was six or eight days' travel behind Spc\er s party, and it was supposed that he could not overtake them. Mr. Howard, the gentleman despatched bv Government on a special mission to New Mexico, was met on the Kith, at the crossing of the Arkansas, with his pack mules broken down. He had however, despatched two men as an express to Sante be, on fresh mules, .and they were expected to reach there in nine

days From thence they were to return to the foot of the Taos mountains where Mr. Howard was to await their coming Mr Bent saw on the route one hundred and thirlv wagons, belonging to the traders. He also met two long trains of provision wagons þÿ the first within twenty five miles of Council Grove and the other at Dragon creek. They were ordered to stop at Fort Bent, where it is understood the whole expedition will rendezvous. The trade in New Mexico was doll, nor was it likely to be better during the present year. Archuleta, the former commandant of New Mexico, died on the 23d ol May, at banta Fe. Mr. Bent estimates lite population of New Mexico at between thirty and forty thousand of whom 25.000 reside east and north of the Ilio del Norte.

Tiieaty witii the Pottawatomie Indians þÿ The Lexington Telegraph ol ihe 23d says: þÿ The commissioners, Major Andrews, U. S A., Major Harvey, superintendent of Indian affairs, and Mr. Matlack. who were charged with making a treaty with the Pottawatomie Indians, passed through this place on Saturday last on their way homeward. We learn tltat a treaty had been effected by which the Pottawatomie cede to the United States four millions of acres of land lying between the Mississippi and Missouri rivers, in t lie territory of Iowa and the disputed tract ; and also about one million of acres lying on the waters of the Osage, South and West of the state of Missouri. The Pottnwatomies are bv this treaty to be united in one body, and lucaied on the

ST $ m t>'iZ A'T'JtS. east end of the lands purchased front the Kansas last winter; half a million of acres of which are granted litem by the treaty together with an annuity of some thirty thousand dollars to continue for thirty years, and possibly longer, under certain contingencies. There are several small tribes of Indians, scalteiing bands, under different names, but all belonging to the Pottawatomie tribe, who will be united by litis treaty, and located permanently on a body of land comprising half a million of acres, which, with the annuity they are to receive, must make them more comfortable than heretofore.

THE CARNIVAL AT LISBON. We copy the following account of the proceedings of the Carnival lately held in this city, from the private correspondence of a daily paper. We trust the time is not far distant when such semi barbarous and disgraceful festivals will be put " The Ungraceful mirth of our Lisbon earnival was not altered in the least for i fie better this year, but considerably lor the worse, notwithstanding the solemn injunction of t he new Cardinal Patriarch. The imaginative resources of this period consist it) several thousands of people pelting each other lor many successive days with beans, rotten eggs, dead rats, soot, and water. The si reels during the past week have been strewn with beans which, if not thus squandered, might have afforded a meal to every poor person in t lie metropolis. Dead and een live rata have been let down from windows at intervals ii pou ji lie heads of the passengers. Prom my balcony I reckoned 12 dozen of eggs which were flung within a lew hours on the (Sunday before Lent. The walis were all plastered with the yolks, where they did not decorate Lisboniau noses. Many young leilows of taste pouted dozens of them in sue cession into the windows of their inamoiaias þÿ an odd way of bringing them into subjection to the 'matrimonial yoke.' 'I hey were even visibly egged on by Ihe smiles of old maids and matrons who should have known better. Not a single lady was able to go to Divine Service on the Sunday, and the English Church was nearly deserted. A deluge of

soot or flour does not improve Parisian bonnets. In a central street, near the Chagas, a man thus foolishly engaged lost his balance while playing the entrudo, as they call it, or ' intruding' his boisterous mirth upon the passengers. He had stretched out too far in flinging a handful of beans, fell into the street from an upper window, and vvas killed on the spot. The masked balls at Oporto, which were merely licentious, have been stopped by the authorities. This judicious measure of police produced a great outcry, something approaching to what might be apprehended in Spain of bull-fights were suppressed ; but the outcry was chiefly confined to the scum of the community. A club of young men, resembling that of Purtido del Vrue.no , or ' Thunder ('tub, of which Gonzales Bravo was a leading member, at Madrid, traversed the streets of Lisbon for the three days preceding Ash Wednesday, accompanied by servants carrying baskets of eggs, and even followed by srges, or hackney cabs, in which were other basketful! of these disgusting missiles, and indulged themselves with the Hottentot amusement þÿ I beg the ' Hottentots' pardon, the cavalleresque amusement þÿ I of flinging them with all their force at the

þÿwindows and balconies as tbev passed aiong. It is impossible to desct ihe the hideous appearance which the walls and windows of the metropolis thus plasteied presented þÿ The contemptuous waste of food was illus trated by a barbarous indifference to the appeals of human distiess; and one young sprig of nobility, while in the act of removing in a basket from a ienda, or chandler's shop, all the eggs which it contained, to be used as missiles, was implored by a beggarwoman for a solitary cupper, which he refused ! In addition to the loss of life which I have already recorded, 1 am informed that the life of a woman was sacrificed through a fall, occasioned by her stepping hack in fright, upon seeing one of these Bayards firing at her. Many ladies of respectability h id eggs burst full in their faces, a id one was seriously hurt on the tcni| I Otheis who ventured into the streets upon the early days had live rats and mice let down by strings on their an end to: þÿ bonnets and shoulders! " The good people of Oporto, disappointed of their masked ball by the intervention of the authorities, avenged themselves by a very pleasant pantomime pasquinade þÿ Amongst the numerous masks who paraded the streets of the town on Stndav night was a roam! do/, n unayed in cloaks and slouched bats, who went in a body, looking over their shoulders every instant, and apparently in the utmost dread of recognition. Upon their hacks each bore the following placard: þÿ ' We are eonspiiutors þÿ don't tell the police'!"

All that are too fond of wine, Or any other stuff, Take warning by the dismal fate Of one Lieutenant Luff. A sober man he might have been Except in one regard þÿ He did not like soft water, So he took to drinking hard.

Said he, let others fancy slops, And talk in praise of tea ; But 1 am no Bi.hea man, So 1 do not like Buhea : If wine's a poison, so is tea, Though in another shape; What matters whether one is killed. By cannister or grape,-

According to this kind of taste He did indulge his drought. And being fond ol port, he made A pot t hole of bis mouth ! A single pint he inijjht have sipped, Anil not been out of sorts, In geologic phrase, the rock He split upon was quarts I

To " hold the mirror up to vice," With him was hard, alas ! The worse lor wine he often was But not ' before a glass-'1 No kind and prudent friend lie had To bid tiini drink no more; The only cA< quers in Ins course Were at the tavern door !

Full soon the sad effects of this His frame began to show, For that old enemy, the gout, Had taken him in toe I And, joined with this, an evil came Of quite another sort ; For while be drank himself, bis purse Was getting " something short."

For want of cash he soon had pawned One half that he possessed ; And drinking showed him duplicates, Beforehand of the rest. So now his creditors resolved To seize on Ins assets, For why, they found that his half pay Did not half pay his debts.

But Luff contrived a novel mode His creditors to chouse, For his own execution lie But into his own house ! A pistol, to the muzzle charged, He took, devoid of fear. Said he, " I'liis barrel is mv last, So uow for my last bier."

Against his lungs he aimed the slugs, And not against his brain : So he blow out his light, and none L'nuld blow them in again ! A jury for a verdict met, And gave it in these terms: " We find as how as certain slugs lias sent him to the wor ms." , þÿ þÿ»oc-o» An Indian chief being asked his opinion of a jog of rum, said he thought it must be the juice of women's tongues, and lion's hearts, for alter drinking it he could talk forever, and fight the devil.

Is Sante Fe a part of the United States or not? þÿ We have already had occasion to notice the singular conduct of the government, in regard to the trade to Sante Fe and New Mexico. The law recognizes Sante Fe as a part of the teriitory of a foreign government. To encourage the trade of our citizens with that country, a drawback was allowed upon all goods imported to ihe United Slates, and afterward expoi ted in the original packages to New Mexico. This law, and the refunding duties under it, had been recognised at the Treasury Department, up to a very recent period. When, however, it had become necessary to assert our title to the whole of the country East of the lliu Grande, following that river to its extreme length, Sante Fe became thereby part a of the United States, and the absurdity of the law, or of the claim to the territory, became at once appaient. In this dilemma, the Secretary of the Treasury determined to assert the possession of the territory, by refusing to recognize the provisions of ihe law, in regard to drawback as applicable to Sante Fe. There were large amounts of goods in the public warehouses at New York, which the owners refused to take uniil the Collector would issue the necessary debenture certificates, lie declined to do so, under orders, and it is said the matter was referred to a Cabinet council at Washington, hn their decision. We now understand that the Collector lias been made to take the back liuck, and, as a necessary

consequence, it follows tiiat Mr. Folk's admiiiistiation recognizes Sante Fe, though claimed by the 1'icsident as within the territorial boundaries of the United Slates, as really forming a part of the Mexican Kcpublie. A gentleman, who is acquainted with all the facts, has handed us a note, in which it is said þÿ " 1 lie goods ol certain Mexican merchants of Chihuahua, which had her n detained at the custom house in New York for some time, in consequence of a relusal to issue debenture certificates, have been released, and the certificates granted. These gentlemen, who have been here for son.e time awaiting the result, rue to leave to day (yesterday) lor Independence, to get their outfit ready, preparatory to their leaving lor Santc Fe." These proceedings on the part of the government involve the grossest absurdities. The ownership of the territory of the Bio Grande is claimed by the Fiesident and all his followers. It was made the preiext for ordering Gen. Taylor to remove his forces from Corpus Clirisli, and to take up a posnh n in fiont ol Matanioros, and to repel by lone any troops who might attempt to cross that boundary. Gen. Taylor did so repel tin m and defeated and followed the invaders to their own territoiy. Now, however, the administration refuses to assert claim to the same boundary at .Santo Fe, as well marked on the map as that of the Bio Grande at Maiamoros, and actually recognizes its existence as a part of the Mexican territory- Not only has this been done in the particular ease
to wh o.h we have referred, hut the American government now has a cousul at Sante he, (Mr. Alvarez ) and it is only a few weeks since lire consular seal was sent to him by
order of the government ! What can we expect from an administration which so involves itself in contradictions and absurdities as to make it the laughing stock of the whole country.

The double door, opened at an angle to admit the air, gives glimpses of deep brunettes, throwing retrarkablyluxuriantandd.uk tresses over their heads, previous to arranging them for the evening lisilessness. Men sit sullenly about in their fantastic dresses, half of tliern looking as if they had been stolen from a stock company of a theatre while engaged in playing a " brigand piece.'" There is a flaunting, stilletlo-y ou-in-lhe-dai k e .pression about them. As you wander on you find the city remarkably well laid out, and although giving evidences of having seen better days, still it is far from being desti" te of attractive buildings Once fairly in the l'ltizu Hidalgo, the pi incipal square of the city, you can rest youtself under the shade of some stunted China trees, and then commence examining at your leisure. You will at once be attracted by the un-

finished 'Jaihedial, which is so managed that the houses on its wings appear to he part of the Cathedral itself giving to the mass a very imposing appearance ; it bounds one entire side of the plaza. Two fine but unfinished towers command the sides of the Cathedral, upon o.ie of which is rudely laid n piece of timber from which are suspended a couple of hells. The large gothic door in the centre would have exposed the interior with great effect, but alas, some misfortune overwhelmed its progress, and left the hare walls to provoke t he imagination into contemplating the rea sons why a work so well begun was not completed. In front, seated in the angles formed by the bases of the pillars, or upon the bases themselves, are fifty or moie poor miserable creatures, who seem, in their poverty, to have nothing in abundance but sunshine, and that they ate determined to enjoy. Few well d'essed persons linger in their vicinity, hut pass decorously on and disappear in a narrow alley way on the right of lite Cathedral, where we enter. Finding himself worn down by the infirmities el age, Sedgewold oidered Ins three daughters tirto his presence, and tiestowed on every one her sti.rre in his proper tv, trior ea trie and immoveable, and thus admessed them : "1 have a diamond of immense value: it shall he given to Iter who, in the course of the year, shall have pet formed the most generous action." At the end of the year, on the day he had specified, Sedgewold beheld his three daughters arrive. " Father," said the eldest, " by chance 1 discovered an important secret, which, to have revealed, would have made my lot tune forever. 1 resisted this temptation, to follow the severe voice of probity." " You have done your duty my child," replied Sedgewold; "a different conduct would have rendered you a disgrace to your parent." " Father," said the second daughter, " I had two neighbors, who were honest men and exemplary husbands: a long series of misfortunes obliged them to break their pro mises : 1 sunk a patt of my fortune to stop the put suits of their creditors, and ie-establish them in business " "You did well, my daughter," said Sedgewold ; but you have already received your recompense by the pleasure that you have had in well doing." Adela, the youngest of the three, expressed het self as lollow s : "1 loved an amiable man who returned my love : his name was Alphonso. Josephine,

my friend from early childhood, became fatally enamored of him : she strove against her passion, but I saw her sinking into the grave þÿ the rose fled ftom her blooming cheek, her eyes lost all their brilliancy, and she wasted to a skeleton. One day, as I fix ed niv eyes on her countenance, my tears proved to her how much I was affected to see her so changed; and Josephine, sensible of the friendship 1 felt for her, wept as she embraced me: ' Too kind and too generous

.i, 1 1 frier.d," said she, 'it is too þÿlate death is here,' added she, putting her hand on her heart. I made use of all the eloquence of friendship, caresses and teats; Josephine consented often to come and see me, and by degrees her health was re established 1 rejoiced in what 1 considered as my own work ; but my heart was a prey to a thousand secret sorrows, and 1 became truly a sulfmer n the mean lime, Alphonso complained of my indifference, while never had I loved him so sincerely. Whatever were my own sufferings. I did not fail, nevertheless, to extol, as much as possible, the attractions of Josephine, while 1 taught her to dis phiy all the graces ol her person, nnd she soon appeared what Nature made her þÿ lovely, most charming. Sometimes mv courage would forsake me, but when I cast my eyes upon my friend my reason was instantly restored ; but oh ! the teats that 1 shed in solitude ! At length, Josephine was made happy: Alphonso, petsunded that f no It nuer loved him. rev, nged himself on my pretended fickleness, by paving his addresses to her. I immediately made a pretext that travelling was requisite for my health; hut before my depaittne I requ s'ed my friend to hasten her marriage as speedilv as possible In about a month alter, she w rote to inlortn rne that it had taken place. What n letter! never shall I forget it; it w.i.s scarcely legible þÿ her tears having effaced almost all the characters, i returned to the place ol her habitation to see her, to embrace her, and wish her that happiness that

can never he mine. I then came back to you, not to receive the rewind of my sacrifice, for what recompense can I obtain, hut the pleasure of having obeyed my father " hfere is the ring." said Sedge wold. þÿ " Your action, my dear daughter, was truly generous, since you have sacrificed the tenderest of passions þÿ a passion which often conquers the wis st of mankind þÿ to make your friend happy but, my dear Adela. trust in mv experience þÿ you will cute youiscl! of a tenderness, the most ol which you have destroyed, by depriving it of hope ; and the hand ot a worthy man will dry up the tears of disappointed love."

Private letters from Kotne of the 29ih alt, announces that « Ire six cardinals comprising the temporary commission of government had disagreed among themselves, and that Cardinals Lambruschini, Mallei, and Bernetii had tendered iheir resignation. A full amnesty was to be published in a few days. þÿ The Pope signed on the 28th the pardon ol Professor Orioli, Minister of Public Instruction during the revolution of 1831. His Holiness intended to permit the construction of railroads through the Papal dominions, and to introduce various reforms in the ad ministration. Several inhabitants of Home having been arrested, and the Governor being unable to assign any satisfactory reason for that measure, the Pope ordered the prisoners to be immediately restored to liberty. þÿ The Military Commissions of Bologna, Ravenna, and Rimini had been dissolved. A negative reply had been returned to the note. A f.GERI V. Wc regret to find that the war between the French and the Arab tribes is still marked by the most atrocious and revolting cruelty. Accounts from Oran mention that dispatches have been received from General Cavuignae,

the commander in chief of the division of I he army stationed at Djentma Ghazaouat, which stale thai the Arabs, taking advantage of the temporary absence of the general made a how of attacking some detachments of troops employed in repairing the road between Gbazaouat and the frontier. The troops immediately ceased working, and sent an express to General Cavaignae, with an account of the apprehended danger. General t.nvaignac immediately returned with the detachment under his command, and contrived to get the Arabs between his column and the sea, so that they could not hv any possibility escape. He then attacked them fiercely, and the wretched houle of Arabs (500 in number) were butchered to a man. The greater portion were destroyed by the fire of the troops, and the remainder were driven into the sea and drowned. Of the French there does not appear to have been a man killed or wounded. þÿ Ibid.

The Washington correspondent of the Baltimore But riot gives the tollowtng account of the combat : þÿ The quarrel had gone on in their news papers to such an extent that Mr. Pleasants thought himself called upon to bring the matter to a ciisis. He thereiore sent a request to Mr. Ritchie to meet him at a specified place and hour across the river from Richmond, with side aims. Mr. Ritchie sent word back that he could not consent to settle the affair in that way. Mr. Pleasants then sent him word that the matter must he settled, and in that way. Mr, Ritchie then prepared himself with a revolver of six barrels, two duelling pistols, and a horseman's short sword, and repaired to the place designated at the time named. Mr. Pleasants arrived, with two (or four there is a doubt about this) common pistols and a sword cane. A triend of Mr Pleasants approached Mr. Ritchie, and said to him th A he thought the difficulty might he settled if the latter would do one thing þÿ acknowledge that he believed Mr Pleasants to be a biave man. Mr. Ritchie replied that once he could have done this, but now, Mr. Pleasants having called him there, lie could not make such an acknowledgment. Soon after ibis Mr. Pleasants approached Mr. Ritchie, considerably in advance of the two fi iends who had accompanied him to the spot. As lie approached at a rapid pace Mr. Ritchie fiied successively his two duelling pistols resting each on Ins left arm, drawn up in an angle for that put pose. He

then presented his revolver and bred edher four or five of its barrels. After he had fired first upon Mr. Pleasants the latter drew and fired thrice without effect all the time rushing up to Mr. Ritchie, and when near enough he struck linn with his sword cane, when the scabbard flew oil, and Mr Ritchie struck up the blade or spear with bis short sword, in doing which lie received the point in the corner of his mouth, culling upward a slight gash. Mr. Pleasants then fell, having received five wounds, one ball raked across the back of his left hand, carrying away all the muscles and tendons leading to the lingers another passed through the fleshy part of lus leii arm, half way up from the elbow to the shoulder Another entered the left breast, and ranged round under the arm. A fourth entered the left groin, and proved mortal. The filth wound was in the right þÿthigh either by a ball or thrust from the short sword. So has ended (lie earthly career of the gifted, the high minded, the generous, whole souled John Hampden Pleasants! His loss to the community in which he moved, to the editorial fraternity of which he was ever a sparkling, brilliant member, and to the thousands of his ever delighted and instiucted readers, will he must deeply felt, as his sanguinary exit will ho sadly mourned. For many years he has been one of the most vigorous, original, and brilliant political writers in the country. He was a man of strong impulses, and, in the excitement of the moment, sometimes committed editor iat
errors, or did his opponents injustice ; but that man lived not who would more readily or amply atone for indiscretions or injuries ol this nature.

We received per Severn , a file of the Morning Journal to the 8th inst. 1 lie news from Mexico, which we give hcnealh will be found interesting, but the local news Ironi the above island is this time very meagre : From the Jamaica Morning Journals The lloyal Mail Company's steamer Avon has brought us papers from Bermuda, Honduras, and Turks island. 1 he Company s steamer Clyde has arrived at Bermuda from Vera Cruz. The news bv her is very important, particularly as relates to the Californias placing themselves under the protection of the U. States of America, intelligence of which was brought to this island by Her þÿMajesty sbrig Daring The Clyde was refused permission by the American blockading Squadron to land her outward freight of quicksilver at Tampico, and she was compelled to carry it to Vera Cruz. The following is a summary of the news from Mexico: þÿ The Mexican Congress was installed on the 6th of June; Gen. Paredes, elected President ; Gen. Bravo, Vice President of the Republic. The Californios had declared their independence of Mexico through American intrigue. The States of Durango and Chihuahua were in revolt against the Government, and were about to form an independent Republic under the title of the Republic of the Rio Grande, to be protected by America. General Taylor had occupied the villages on the right bank of the Rio Grande, and was about to advance on Sattille, and Irom thence he would march direct on Mexico.

Vera Cruz was declared in a state of siege, and martiai law proclaimed on the 30th June, as it was generally supposed that the American squadron would attack the Castle of San Juan de Ulloa on the 10th instant. The Biitish and Foreign Merchants and the greater portion of the respectable Mexican families had left Vera Cruz and 1 ampico for the interior. B Russ b i. s, Thursday July 11. On Wednesday afternoon, the 8th instant a most calamitous occurrence, accompanied by a fearful sacrifice of human life occurred

on the Great North of France Ba Iway, better known as the Parts and Brussels Railway. The scene ol the accident is situated on the frontier of Belgium and France, between the stations Aras arid Dome As may be supposed in such cases, the most conflc'ing statements are in circulation. From the latest and most authentic sources it would appear that the engine ran off the line, and broke the barrier that protected the banks, try which means two or three of the passenger carriages were mum rsed in a considerable depth ol water below. Not less than 19 persons, it Iras been ascertained, have lost their lives, and it is said that about sixty others have been severely injured or wounded. The water at the piaee of the tragic occurrence vanes in depth irom twelve to fifteen feel, and ike descent from the line is almost perpendicular. The first intelligence that reached Brussels (some fifty miles distant from the scene of the accident) was conveyed by a down train, which was due at s ven o'clock on Wed ne day but which did not arrive at Brussels until about six þÿo clock on the following morning. By the concurrent testimony of all parties, the accident is one of a most tragic, and disastrous character resembling in its consequences the accident which occurred s ane live years ago, on the line between Paris and Versailles. 'I he utmost consternation was occasioned in Brussels by the melancholy intelligence, which was represented as having been caused by tire collision of two trains Another

version of the story represented that the accident was occasioned by the falling of one of the arches of tire bridge w hile the train was in the act of passing over: but from subsequent inquiries and information elicited from the passengers who arrived hv the first train, it would appear that the engine which was proceeding at a rate far interior to that usually adopted upon English railways;, ran oil the tramway or cltemin de fer , while passing a bridge, burst through a low parapet wall, and þÿw ns precipitated headlong into tl e water. This sad calamity lias served to throw a considerable gloom over the city of Brussels, and especially amongst the English inhabitants, many of whom were expecting friends by the ill (fated conveyance. Meantime Texas, by the final action of our Congress, had become an integral part of our Union. The Congress of Texas, by its act of December 10, 1836, had declared the llio del Norte to be the boundary of that republic. Its jurisdiction had been extended and exercised beyond the Nueces. The country between that river and the Del Norte had been represented in the congress and in the convention of Texas; had thus taken part in the act of annexation itself; and is now included within one ot our congressional districts Our own Congress had, moreover, with great unanimity, by the act approved December 31, 1845, recognised the country beyond the Nueces as a part of our territoiv, by including it within our own revenue svstem ; and a revenue officer, to reside within that district, has been appointed, by an«l with the advice and consent of the Senate. It became, therefore, of urgent necessity to provide for the defence of that portion of our country, Accordingly, on the 13th of January last, instructions were issued to the general in command of these troops to occupy the left bank of the Del Norte. This river, which is the southwestern boundary of the Stale of Texas, is an exposed frontier; from this quarter invasion was threatened ; upon it, and in its immcdi ate vicinity, in the judgment of high military experience, are the proper stations for the protecting forces of the government. The movement of the troops to the Del Norte was made by I Ire commanding general, Under positive instructions to abstain from all aggressive acts towards Mexico or Mexican citizens, and to regard t he relations between that republic and the United States as peaceful, unless site should declare war, or commit nets of hostility indicative of a state of war. lie was specially directed to protect private property, and respect personal rights. This mail brings the intelligence of tlie commencement of war between Mexico ami the United States, with the proclamation of the President formally declaring war, and willi tiis message in justification ol it It appeals thai ihe Mexican government has already captured a detachment of Aineiican troops It is a matter ot very little moment to ibis country ; Mexico has no force with which to contend with the United Stales, and the matter must very shortly end It is no concern of ours, except the President should proceed so far as to conquer and incorporate Mexico with the United States: it may then become a question whether it is consistent with sound policy to peimit this extinction of an independent government, and ti e consequent aggrandisement ot the United States. THE REVOLUTION IN PORTUGAL. RESIGNATION OF THE MINISTRY. By intelligence just received from Lisbon we learn that, so far from tlie revolution having been suppressed, it has extended over neatly the whole country, the soldiers in ir.ost instances sympathising with the people, and both demanding the dismissal of the Costa Caliral Ministry. The young Count Villa Real is at the head of the insurgeants in Ties os Monies, where 800 nieu are under arms, and a political junta has been formed. I lie Minister of justice (M. J. Cnbral), who had been sent to Oporto, invested with diciatmial powers to put down the insurrection in that district, tiad been obliged to on board a steamer, and return to Lisbon. make Ins escape - On the following <h»\ the whole ol the ministers, seeing the a '.aiming aspect ot allatis,

fchi! being abandoned to so great an extertl by Una army, tendered their resignations to her Majesty, by Whom they were accepted ; and Count Villa lveal was charged with the formation of a new Cabinet. The Count, lioweveiy soon gave tip the task as a hopeless one, and the Duke of Palmella has undertaken it ; with what success remains to be seen. We have seen a private letter winch represents the movement to be of a very formidable character, and likely to lead to important results, as the people seem thoroughly determined to rid themselves to a gieat eX tent of the heavy burdens imposed upon them to pay the interest of the enormous debt contracted in establishing the present dynasty upon the throne. Should they succeed in this object, the holders of l'oituguese slock Will be the sufferers. þÿ þÿ-»ooo ESCAPE Ob LOUIS ISA POL LOIS FROM HAM. Prinee Louis Napoleon has escaped from his prison at Ham. and has arrived in Lotr don. The National gives the following account of the escape : þÿ The prisoners and the commandant of the' fortress had for some time represented rhe necessity of some repairs in that part which was occupied by Prince l.ouis , the board of engineers had or dered them to be done, and men were at work in the rorridor leading to the apartments of the prisoners. þÿ On Monday morning, between six and seven o'clock, the prince pot on the dress ol a labourer, came quietly out of his chamber, and made his way into the street without being recognised bv any one. As the keep-

els came in the usual manner to ascertain that he was still in their custody, he, in order to delude them, had placed a lay figure in his hed ; but as the governor also was in the habit of visiting and conversing with the prince, it was necessary to provide lor this emergency, and the governor is said to have given the following account of the manner in which he was deceived. Going about nine o'clock to see his prisoner, the physician C þÿ , the intimate friend and companion of the Prince, met the commandant at the door, and, with a disturbed countenance, told him that the Prince had in the night a most dreadful attack of illness, but was a little better, and was then asleep, adding that he had been subject to alarming symptoms for some time, which had become so much aggravated that it imposed a duty on the commandant to recommend his release as soon as possible, otherwise Iris charge would languish and die under his confinement. The commandant promised to make the government fully acquainted with the state of the Prince, and retired. At one in the afternoon the commandant returned again to his prisoner's lodgings to inquire how he then was ; hut the doctor again opposed his entrance into the prisoner's chamber, saying that he had iust taken a powerful medicine. M. de Maine again withdrew till four o'clock, when on presenting himself once more, the doctor opened the door, saying, 'You may now come in, for the Prince is gone.' Enlightened at once on the trick that had been played

upon him, the commandant instituted an inquiry, and sent an estaletle to the government. Every onfer was immediately given to seek for the fugitive, but as Ire bad ten hours before him he hud already got out of tire kingdom."

ALGERIA. Marshal Bugeaud will shortly return to France, having resigned the post ol Governor General of Algeria. Nothing is yet determined as to his successor, ar d the new system of government to be applied to Algeria. The French ministry has resolved before coining to any decision to await the debate in the Chamber of Deputies, on the grants of money required for the African possessions. It is generally believed thai some change will take place in t lie system of administration, and that the Governor General, although a general otiicer, will deiive the greater gait of tiis power from the civil authority. General Tiburee Sebasliani, who now commands in Paris, is mentioned as the probably successor of Marshal Bugeaud.

The I'hare ties Pyrenees gives the following rather incredible account of an affair which, it says, had just occurred in one of die valleys of Navarre, near the French frontier : þÿ ' A few days since an individual in female apparel entered a lone house and demanded hospitality. The inhabitants ol the house consisted of a man, his wife, and a young child. They soon discovered that their guest was no other than a man in disguise, and as night was approaching, the husband not liking the appearance of his guest, went out at a back door to seek assistance from the nearest neighbour. During his absence the wife became alarmed, and went into an ad joining room, the door of which she fastened' The man wished to follow her, but being unable to do so, told her at once the object of his visi', which was to possess himself of the sum of money which they had received for ihe sale of corn a few days before, and threatened, if it was refused to kill her child, which, in her fright, she had If ft in the room with him. The poor woman, not imagining that ho would commit such a crime, and being in n omental y expectation of her husband's return, still refused to open the door. The screams of her child, however. so,>n told her that the wretch had carried his tin en ts into execution Having accomplished the deed of blood by cutting the poor little orea-

- - - . - lure's throat, he again endeavored to open the door of the room in which the woman had taken refuge, but not being able to afloet his purpose, he broke a hole in the partition, through which he began to lorce himself. On seeing his head, through the aperture, the woman, in a fit of desperation, seized him by the hair, and, with a reaping hook, which, fortunately for her lay within reach, actually cut of? his head. The husband soon after returned, and his horror may be imagined on seeing his child with its throat cut, and the headless trunk of his treacherous guest ly ing in a pool of blood, and, in the next room his wife in a swoon, with a human head at her feet !"

Lightning Rous. þÿ In a recent communication in the Newhaven Courier, respecting some recent instances of houses being struck by lightning, Professor Sillinian suites that the lightning rods cannot be relied upon unless they reach the eaith, where it is permanently wet, even in times of the severest drought ; and that the best security is afforded by carrying the rod, or some good metallic conductor duly connected with it, to the water in the well, or to some other water that never fails. Professor Sillunan's house, it seems, was struck ; hut his lightning rods wore not more than two or three inches in the ground, and vveie therefore vutually of no avail in protecting the house He states that his confidence in t tie efficiency of rods is in no degree diminished. þÿ New Yoik Observer.

At ten minutes to six þÿo clock on the evening ol the 25th ult. the whole city seemed suddenly to undulate, as it rolling upon a heavy sea, and, though there was not a bieaffi of wind, the water in the boy was violently agitated The windows rattled as if in a strong gale, doors were suddenly burst open, and then dashed to with violence. LORD JO H A RUSSELL'S SPEECH TO Ills CONSTITUENTS. Gentlemen, þÿ The administration of Sir Robert Peel having been dissolved her Majesty has been pleased to confer cn me the office of First l.ord of the Treasury; mv sea! in Parliament lias therefore become vacant, and is again at your disposal. þÿ When you did me the honor to ask me to represent you, 1 consented to become a candidate, not merely or chiefly because the distinction of representing the City of London was a just object ol ambition, but be cause 1 wished to obtain for the principles of commeicial freedom the sanction of your approbation. Although 1 was elected by a very small majority and the elections of 1841 were adverse to my hopes, and favorable to the doctrines of protection, every year that lias since elapsed has witnessed some relaxation of restriction, and some advance towards the establishment of the principle for which 1 have contended.

t'inally, we have this year seen Sir Robt. Veel propose and carry a measure lor a total repeal of the duties upon foreign corn. You may be assured, that 1 shall not desert in office the principles to which I adhered when they W'ere less favourably received, i cannot indeed, claim the merit cither of having carried measures of tree trade as a Minister, or of having so prepared the public mind by any exertion of mine as to convert what would have been an impracticable attempt into a Certain victory. To others belong those distinctions. Hut l have endeavored to do my part in the great work according to my means arid my Convictions; first by proposing a temperate relaxation of the Corn laws, and afterwards when that measure had been repeatedly rejected, bv declaring in favour -of total repeal, and using any influence I Could exert to prevent a continuance of the snuggle lor an object not worth the cost of a conflict. 1 trust that the measures of commercial freedom which still remain to he accomplished will not occasion the renewal of angry conflict. The Government of this country ought to behold with an impartial eye the various portions of the community engaged m agriculture, in manufactures, and in commerce. The feeling that auv one of them is treated with injustice provokes ill-will, disturbs legislation, and diverts aitention tri m many useful and necessary reforms. Great social improvements are required: public education is lamentably deficient, the treatment of criminals is a problem vet to he solv.

ed ; the sanatory condition of our towns and villages has been grossly neglected : ihe administration of our colonies demands the most earnest and deliberate attention. Our recent discussions have laid bare the misery, the discontent, and outrages of Iteland ; they are too clearly authenticated to tie denied; too extensive to be treated by any but the most comprehensive measures. Should you again elect me your member, it will be my duty to consider all these important matters in conjunction with those whoifi her Majesty has been pleased to call to her councils. At the present moment nnv further explanation of my views would be unauthorised and þÿimperfect. 1 have the honor to be, your most faithful and obedient servant. J- Russell.

A new Way op raising the Wind. þÿ Among Hie merchants ot this country, and especially ol Liverpool, there has been a pietty general complaint of the inconveniences that arise from the practices of a class of shipping agents. These persons, it seems, are in the habit of bespeaking beforehand all the height room in some ol the tiunsatlati'ic steamers, and then retail it at a profit to parties who want to ship their goods, completely excluding them unless they will consent to liteir terms. The evil thus complained ol, which consists in the important article of freight being left at the mercy of a lew interested individuals, is, of course, intelligible enough, but it is not so easy to sec how it is to be avoided. If one person chooses to engage a large number of cubic feet on board a particular vessel, the owner of that vessel will sea i cel y refuse him, unless there is something manifestly wrong in the transaction ; and the purchaser of this quantity of room has so much disposable propeity. which he can sell at his own price The same thing happens in t lie case of passengers when the owners of the vessels sell tickets for a certain number of berths, but have no power to prevent them being retained, and consequently it is possible lor a person who buys up the berths early, to sell them at a profit. In some of the foreign ports, which are much less extensive than those ol London, the evil has been obviated by the exertions of the þÿshipowners agents. Being able to ascertain

in a limited community the absolute wants of the proportion of room which each ought to have, atid peremptorily to refuse exceeding the limit they have fixed. But in a large metropolis like London the knowledge which is necessary to take precautionary measures of the sort is absolutely unattainable ; and suppose, for instance, it were a fixed regula' tion that no one person or firm should have more than a certain amount of accommodation, those who wished still to pursue the practice intended to he obviated could easily frustrate the vigilance of the company with a list of names got up for the occasion. It the abuse were removed, it would no doubt confer a benefit on the community, but it seems extremely hard to make out a definite case for legislative interference. þÿ London Fnper,

We have much pleasure in laying before onr readers Ibe following document, issued by the Turkish Grand Vizier, on the subject of the persecution to which the Armenian Protestants in various parts of the empire have lately been exposed by the arbitrary conduct of their ecclesiastical rulers. Eor the first time, hut most decidedly, the reformation of the sixteenth century is officially acknowledged bv the Porte as n re cognised form of Christianity, and placed virtually on as independent a base as that of either the Greek or Kentish Church Pro lestiinism is now planted in the Ottoman empire, and it is onr hope and belief that it will strike its roots deep and spread them wide. We will not, however, enter into any of the many reflections the subject suggests, hut will at once transcribe the vizciial letter : þÿ þÿ copy of Tim vizr.it i a i, litter to ii. e. the paciia op riH/.nitmM « A , an Armenian, of Eizeronm, a subject of the Sublime Porte, having left bis former belief, and gone over by the Protest-

unt faith, and there being some persons among the Armenians in that quarter, suffering various forms of oppression and persecution, he lias come to Constantinople, and presented a petition, begging that a slop may be put to the persecution. þÿ Now. as is well known to your Excellency. for some time past, the Protestant faith has spread in some degree among the Armenians. In Constantinople, also, a number ol the Armenian community having embraced the Protestant faith, and having been anathematised by their patriarch, the Armenians in consequence retuseu to have social or commercial intercourse with them or to become their sureties. And as the persons the excommunicated presented from oilier communities weie not accepted, a complete stagnation in their trade and business was the result, and their shops were closed. þÿ Now, although nothing be said, if in consequence of the spiritual penalties of t fie Patriarch, the Armenians cannot trade wuh them or become their sureties, theie has, however, emanated an expression of the royal will of Ins Imperial Majesty the Sultan on this subject, ordering that the Patriarch should be forbidden to interfere in their personal or religious affairs, and that all the authorities concerned, when sureties were offered by them from among the various communities, should accept them, and that llms there should be no hmdiance to iheir pm suing their occupations and gaining liimr living. þÿ As this order has been put in execution

here, their troubles have therefore, in some measure, ceased. In case, then, there are similar individuals under your þÿExcellency s authority, your Excellency will follow tire same rule. þÿ Wherefore, in order that such persons who present sureties from other communities may be permitted to follow iheir trades and occupations, and that the Armenians primates and community may not be suffered in any way to persecute or interfere with them when occupied in their trades and commerce provided then life is decent and orderly, and that they are not guilty of impropei conduct, or do n"t. undei pretence of religion, stir up simple people, this official letter has been written and forwarded, that your Excellency may protect and defend them. A commission was formed, and soon collected the sum necessary to cover the expenses of a statue. 1 he commission then thought U would be well to extend the circle of the subscription and toopply for their concunence to the erection of the projected monument, to the families amongst the English nobility, whose Norman extraction has not yet been defaced by time. From the above genealogical table, we find that amongst the living princes, it is the Archduke Charles of Austria, so h uiourablv known in the French armv, who is the nearest relative to William the Conqueror (22d degree), and that the princes of Sweden, the descendants of Prince Maximilian, son of Eugene Beuuharnais. the inheriting Duke of Saxe Weimar, are the most distantly connected (29th degree!. To reach a maximum salary, such as the last-named, requires years of steady perseverance and great abilities for business. The more general average of the salary of the Bank of England ranges from 170/. to 3000/ a year, and this may be rather over than under the mark, considering that, by the recent alteration of the charter, and the separation ot the issue from the deposit department, a number of additional hands were introduced, all at the low rale of salary. A person can never lake office as a Bank of England clerk, till he is 17 years of age, when Ins salary commences at 50/. per year ; and never after 25 years of age, whe he is paid 100/. a year. num, but after that period, the advance is restricted to 8/. per annum.
